accuracy.evidence: Checked against the NC England Y6 evolution and inheritance statements and NGSS 4-LS1-1. Examples verified: fennec fox ears up to about 15 cm used to shed heat and locate prey (Smithsonian National Zoo fennec fox fact sheet); Arctic fox short ears and thick fur reduce heat loss (National Geographic); Arctic cod (Boreogadus saida) antifreeze glycoproteins; camels produce small volumes of highly concentrated urine; finch seed-cracking, hummingbird nectar, raptor hooked beak and dabbling-duck filter bill; mountain hare white winter coat and broad furry hind feet; streamlined bodies reduce drag. The race shows only the order of the shapes; the adult text says so instead of giving invented distances.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented Lamarckian and need-based explanations in children's ideas about adaptation (Driver et al., Making Sense of Secondary Science, ch. on adaptation; AAAS Project 2061 misconception list): 'it stretched its neck and passed it on', 'it decided it needed it', 'it chose to get fat', plus calling every feature structural, treating behaviour as a body part, and thinking big ears keep a fox warm. The hedgehog prediction offers 'not an adaptation: it is just tired'.

lab_distinct.evidence: gate_lab_distinct passed under the 30% shingle limit, including flag_vary.js (beetle variation and bird predation), flag_camo.js, flag_desert.js, flag_polaran.js and flag_pengu.js. No other lab sorts structural, behavioural and physiological adaptations, feeds birds by beak shape, tunes fox ear size against desert and Arctic heat, races block, ball and torpedo shapes through water, or builds a snow animal trait by trait.

lab_teaches.evidence: Six steps: sort six named adaptations into three kinds (wrong bins explain the kind's meaning), match four foods to four drawn beaks, set each fox's ears until both read comfortable, race three body shapes with the same push and compare lane distance, swap four traits to build an animal for deep snow, then the challenge. The learner finds each fit by testing; the banner then names the principle (shape fits job, ears control heat loss, streamlining).

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options: the hedgehog's hibernation as a body part or 'just tired', which fox needs bigger ears (many children pick the Arctic fox for hearing or warmth), and which shape glides furthest (the ball is a common pick). The lab then shows the outcome and the reveal repeats the learner's choice.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions (polar bear fat, swallow migration, Arctic cod antifreeze, seed beak, fennec ears, giraffe necks) with rotated answer order. Ten distinct wrong-answer messages: behaviour versus body part, animals do not choose adaptations, migration is not a body part, physiological means inside processes, antifreeze cannot be seen but is inside the body, nectar beaks, meat beaks, big ears lose heat, stretching is not inherited, needing does not make a feature appear.

readability.evidence: validate_lessons readability passed (kid about 4 and adult about 6.5 by learn/readability.py, limits 6.5 and 9.5). Kid paragraphs use short sentences and named animals; structural, behavioural and physiological are each defined in plain words where first used. Lab banners and messages are one or two sentences.

no_filler.evidence: No filler patterns matched (gate_content). Each kid paragraph has one job: define adaptation and structural, add behavioural and physiological, show shape fitting job with four examples, then explain how features build up over generations. Adult text gives the standards, the checked facts and the named mistakes.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360 × 640 (2x) in light and dark themes for every step. The first sheet showed the hummingbird beak running into its label, birds hidden by the message box and trait cards under the footer; the canvas was made taller (1.4 on phones), bird labels moved to a full-width bottom line, race shapes moved below their lane labels and trait cards moved up. Final sheets show nothing clipped and tap targets at least 36 px tall.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas tap has a button twin (kind buttons for the next card, food-to-bird buttons, smaller/bigger ear buttons for each fox, race buttons, trait swap buttons). The canvas aria-label is rewritten after every action with cards left, birds fed, ear sizes and comfort, race results or the snow animal's traits. The browser gate ran axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) on desktop and iPhone 13 in both themes with no violations; the wrong-path click sweep raised no console errors.
